text: Wireshark is a free, open-source packet analyzer that captures traffic crossing a network interface and lets you inspect every packet in detail. In your isolated lab from the last lesson, open Wireshark on your Kali VM, pick the lab's network interface, and click the shark-fin Start button. Generate some traffic — browse to Metasploitable2's web page, or just let normal background chatter happen — and within seconds the packet list fills with rows, each one a single packet captured the instant it crossed that interface.

A busy capture can fill with thousands of packets, almost all irrelevant to what you're looking for. Display filters narrow the view without discarding anything. tcp.port equals 80 shows only HTTP traffic. ip.addr equals a specific address shows everything touching that one host, in either direction, regardless of protocol or port.

Click any packet and three panes update together. The packet list shows every captured packet, one row each. The packet details pane is where you'll live — it breaks that packet out layer by layer, bottom up: Ethernet frame, then IP addressing, then TCP or UDP ports, then whatever application protocol sits on top. The bytes pane shows the same data as raw hex and ASCII, useful for spotting plaintext credentials.

A healthy TCP connection shows up as exactly three packets: a SYN, a SYN-ACK back, then a final ACK, completing cleanly before real data flows. Something suspicious often breaks that pattern in a specific way — a port scan looks like one source IP firing SYN packets at many different destination ports in rapid succession, with almost none of them getting a SYN-ACK reply at all.

That broken-handshake pattern, or a host quietly beaconing out to the same unfamiliar address on a steady interval, is exactly the kind of signal a real investigation starts from. Next up: tracing one realistic attack stage by stage through the kill chain, and naming the defense at each stage that could have stopped it.
